FMO analysis helped determine the chemical reactivity, softness, hardness, chemical potential, and electrophilic index of the compounds through the HOMO-LUMO energy gap (Egap) parameter. A large Egap indicates high stability and low chemical reactivity, whereas a narrow Egap corresponds to high chemical reactivity and low stability. The energy levels of HOMO and LUMO also play a crucial role in understanding the compounds' electron acceptor and donor properties, respectively, and are critical in chemical reactions. Therefore, FMO analysis is essential for evaluating the reactivity and stability properties of molecules. steps.title: Retrieve flavone derivatives and draw structures
steps.instruction: Search PubChem for flavone and its 14 derivatives (compounds 1‑14), download each SDF file, and open them in ChemDraw to generate 2‑D depictions as shown in Fig. 1.

steps.title: Optimize geometries with Gaussian16
steps.instruction: For each compound (1‑14) run geometry optimizations in Gaussian 16 at three levels of theory: B3LYP/6‑31G(d,p), B3LYP/6‑311G(d,p), and B3LYP/6‑311++G(d,p); perform frequency calculations to confirm true minima; record optimized structures (Tables S1‑S14).

steps.title: Generate FMO and electrostatic maps
steps.instruction: Load each optimized Gaussian output into GaussView 6, visualize HOMO, LUMO, and molecular electrostatic potential (MEP) maps, and export images for the Supplementary Information (Figs. S1‑S18).

steps.title: Calculate dipole moments and descriptors
steps.instruction: From Gaussian 16 log files extract dipole moment and polarization values (Table 1a); compute the following descriptors for each flavonoid using the listed equations: Egap = ELUMO‑EHOMO, IP = ‑EHOMO, EA = ‑ELUMO, χ = (IP+EA)/2, μ = ‑χ, η = (IP‑EA)/2, σ = 1/η, ω = μ²/(2η).

steps.title: Perform single‑point and NBO calculations
steps.instruction: Run single‑point energy calculations and Natural Bond Orbital (NBO) analyses on each optimized structure to obtain accurate energies and atomic charges (as referenced in [57, 58]).

steps.title: Predict ADMET and drug‑likeness
steps.instruction: Enter the canonical SMILES of each flavonoid into SwissADME, admetSAR, and PKCSM web servers; record physicochemical, ADMET, and Lipinski‑rule parameters (Table 2); also run Molinspiration to obtain bioactivity scores for GPCR, KI, ICM, NRL, PI, and EI targets.

steps.title: Run PASS pharmacological predictions
steps.instruction: Upload each flavonoid to the PASS online tool; obtain Pa and Pi values for membrane integrity, permeability inhibition, anticarcinogenic, and antioxidant activities; note compounds with Pa > 0.6 as biologically significant (Table S15).

steps.title: Prepare target protein structures
steps.instruction: Download PDB files for the six proteins: EGFR (4UV7), HER2 (7JXH), FPPS (1YQ7), HPGDS (1V40), DCK (1P60), and Keap1/Nrf2 (1×2J) from the RCSB PDB; validate crystal quality; set histidine protonation; keep default AMBER ff14SB force field; assign Gasteiger charges; remove all ligands, water molecules, and metal ions; add Kollman charges; convert each to PDBQT using AutoDock Tools v1.5.6 (Pyrx).

steps.title: Determine protein active sites
steps.instruction: Submit each PDB file to the CastP server to locate the binding pocket; record pocket surface area and volume (Table 5) and list active‑site residues (Table 6).

steps.title: Prepare ligand files for docking
steps.instruction: Obtain SDF files for the 14 flavonoids plus reference drugs cianidanol and genistein from PubChem; optimize each structure with GaussView 6 and Gaussian 16 at B3LYP/6‑31G(d,p); perform energy minimization; convert the minimized structures to PDBQT using the OpenBabel plugin in PyRx 0.8.

steps.title: Perform molecular docking
steps.instruction: Using AutoDock Vina (via PyRx), dock each ligand (1‑14 and references) into the prepared active sites of the six proteins; record binding affinities in kcal·mol⁻¹ (Table 5).

steps.title: Analyze docking poses and interactions
steps.instruction: Visualize each docked complex with UCSF Chimera, PyMOL v2.5, and BIOVIA Discovery Studio; identify hydrogen bonds, π‑alkyl contacts, and van der Waals interactions; note bond distances (e.g., a 2.207 Å H‑bond in Nrf2‑ligand 7); compile 2‑D interaction diagrams (Figs 3‑4) and list active‑site residues involved (Table 6).

steps.title: Compile results and generate figures
steps.instruction: Assemble all computed data—optimized geometries, FMO/MEP images, descriptor tables, ADMET/physicochemical tables, PASS scores, docking affinities, and interaction diagrams—into the manuscript and Supplementary Information (Figures 1‑4, Tables 1a‑5, S1‑S18).
